title: Linked List Cycle II: find the start of the cycle.
shortTitle: Linked List Cycle II: Find the Start of the Cycle
keyPoints: Phase one uses Floyd's tortoise and hare to find a meeting point inside the cycle
Phase two resets one pointer to the head and advances both by one; they meet at the cycle start
The math: distance from head to cycle start equals distance from meeting point around to cycle start
Runs in O(n) time and O(1) space, needing no hash set or visited markers
Returns null if no cycle exists, detected when fast reaches the end in phase one
The two-to-one speed ratio is what makes the distance equality hold

s1_definition.oneliner: After the tortoise and hare meet inside the loop, move one pointer to the head and step both by one; their next meeting is the cycle's start.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Phase one** – Floyd's detection: slow moves one step, fast moves two steps; if they meet, a cycle exists.
- **Phase two** – reset one pointer to the head, keep the other at the meeting point, advance both by one step; they meet at the cycle entry node.
- **Why it works** – the distance from head to cycle start equals the distance from meeting point to cycle start (modulo loop length), a consequence of the two-to-one speed ratio.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) space.
- **No cycle** – if `fast` reaches null in phase one, return null immediately.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India discovers that a transaction chain has a loop, but needs to find exactly which record the loop re-enters so the repair tool can cut the bad link. Rajesh first catches two fingers inside the loop (phase one), then moves one finger back to the start of the chain and walks both fingers one step at a time. The spot where they meet again is where the loop begins, and that is the link to cut.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Phase 1: Floyd's Detection

  head ──> [A] ──> [B] ──> [C] ──> [D] ──> [E]
                            ▲               │
                            └───────────────┘
  slow and fast start at head
  They meet somewhere inside the cycle (meeting point)

  Phase 2: Find Cycle Start

  entry = head              slow = meeting point
    │                         │
    ▼                         ▼
  [A] ──> [B] ──> [C]       [meeting] ──> ... ──> [C]
                   ▲                               │
                   └── both arrive here ───────────┘

  Distance from head to C  =  Distance from meeting to C
  (around the loop)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Linked List Cycle II finds the exact node where a cycle begins using two elegant phases. In phase one, Floyd's tortoise and hare detect the cycle by moving slow by one and fast by two until they meet inside the loop. In phase two, one pointer resets to the head while the other stays at the meeting point, and both advance one step at a time. They meet at the cycle's entry node.

The mathematics behind phase two is what makes this beautiful. If the distance from head to cycle start is `a`, and the slow pointer traveled `a + b` to the meeting point, then because fast traveled twice as far, `2(a + b) = a + b + nL`, which simplifies to `a = nL - b`. That means the distance from the head to the entry equals the distance from the meeting point around to the entry. Two pointers advancing one step from those two positions will arrive at the same place.

The hash-set alternative finds the start by storing every visited node and returning the first repeat, but it costs O(n) space. Floyd's two-phase method accomplishes the same in O(1) space, which matters in memory-constrained environments like the import pipeline at National Bank of India.

In our banking system, the chain repair tool uses this algorithm after detecting a loop in imported transaction data. It finds the exact re-entry node, sets the offending `next` pointer to `null`, and restores a proper acyclic chain. The same two-phase technique also applies to the "find the duplicate number" problem, where array values are treated as links and a duplicate creates a cycle.

Remember one sentence: after the tortoise and hare meet, reset one to the head, walk both by one, and they meet at the cycle start because `a = nL - b`.
